title: Could You Live Without Your Smartphone for a Month?

warmup.bigQuestion: Could You Live Without Your Smartphone for a Month?

options.text: Yes, but it would be difficult.

reading.title: One Month Without Your Smartphone?
paragraphs: Imagine waking up tomorrow and deciding not to use your smartphone for one month. No social media, maps, mobile banking, music apps, or quick internet searches. You could still use a computer and perhaps a basic phone for calls and texts.
Would this make life better—or simply more difficult?

Smartphones put many useful tools in one place. We use them to stay in touch with friends, check directions, take photos, pay bills, study, work, and solve small problems quickly. For some people, a smartphone is essential because it is their main way to get online.

However, many people also feel that their phones have become a distraction. In a 2026 U.S. survey, 53% of adults said they spent too much time on their smartphones. Forty-five percent said they had tried to reduce their smartphone use during the previous year.

There is also evidence that reducing smartphone internet use may have benefits. In a 2025 experiment, researchers asked people to block mobile internet on their smartphones for two weeks. They could still make calls and send texts, and they could use the internet on other devices. The researchers reported improvements in attention and well-being for many participants. People also spent more time socializing in person, exercising, and being outdoors.
But living without a smartphone is not easy for everyone. Work, transport, banking, family communication, and emergency information may depend on it.
Perhaps the real question is not whether smartphones are good or bad. Maybe the better question is: **Do we control our phones, or do our phones control our time?**

inShort.summary: Smartphones are **convenient** and help us **stay in touch**, but they can also become a **distraction**. Many people want to **cut back on** their **screen time**, although they may still **depend on** their phones for important parts of daily life.

title: Is It Better to Live Alone or With Other People?

warmup.bigQuestion: Is It Better to Live Alone or With Other People?

options.textAr: Living with other people is better.

reading.title: Freedom or Company?
paragraphs: Having your own home can sound perfect. You choose when to eat, when to sleep, how clean the room should be, and what to watch on television. There is no need to explain your choices to anyone else. For many people, living alone means independence and privacy.

But independence has a price. One person must pay the rent, electricity, internet, and other household costs. If something goes wrong, there may be no one at home to help. Some people also feel lonely when they spend too much time by themselves.

Living with other people can solve some of these problems. Roommates or family members can split the bills, share housework, and provide company. A difficult day may feel easier when someone is there to talk to. On the other hand, sharing a home requires compromise. People may have different ideas about noise, visitors, cleaning, food, or personal space.

Research does not show that simply living alone automatically makes someone unhappy. A systematic review found some evidence linking living alone with lower positive mental health, but the authors also stressed that the available evidence was limited and varied. The important point is that “living alone” and “being lonely” are not exactly the same thing.
Some people love having their own space and still have active social lives. Others live in busy homes but still feel alone.
So perhaps the best living arrangement depends less on the number of people in a home and more on personality, money, relationships, and the kind of life a person wants.

inShort.summary: Living alone can offer **independence**, **privacy**, and your own space, while sharing a home can provide company and help people **split the bills**. The best choice often depends on whether people can **get along with** one another and make a **compromise** when their habits are different.

title: Is Online Shopping Better Than Shopping in Stores?

warmup.bigQuestion: Is Online Shopping Better Than Shopping in Stores?

prompts.en: What was the last thing you bought online?
What do you prefer to buy in a physical store?
What can go wrong when you shop online?

reading.title: Click or Walk Into the Store?
paragraphs: Online shopping has changed everyday life. Instead of travelling to several stores, people can compare hundreds of products from a sofa, order at any time, and have purchases delivered to their door. For many customers, this is extremely convenient.

Online marketplaces can also offer a wider selection than a local shop. It is easy to shop around, compare prices, read reviews, and search for a product that may not be available nearby. OECD research notes that digital markets can give consumers greater choice and convenience.

However, convenience does not remove every problem. A product can look different in a photograph, the size may be wrong, delivery can be late, and some reviews can be misleading. Customers may need to send back products they do not want. Fraud and unsafe products are also concerns in some online marketplaces.

Physical stores offer a different experience. Customers can touch a product, try on clothes, ask an employee a question, and take the item home immediately. Shopping in person can also be social. On the other hand, stores have opening hours, limited stock, and sometimes higher prices.

The best choice may depend on the product. Buying a familiar book online is very different from buying shoes that need to fit perfectly. A low price can look attractive, but if a product is difficult to return or is poor quality, it may not be good value after all.
Online and offline shopping are not simply competitors. Many people now move between both, using the internet to research and a store to test—or doing exactly the opposite.

inShort.summary: Online shopping is **convenient**, offers a wide **selection**, and makes it easy to **shop around**. But customers may face **misleading** information, delivery problems, or need to **send back** products that are not **good value**.

title: Should We Spend More Money on Experiences Than Possessions?

warmup.bigQuestion: Should We Spend More Money on Experiences Than Possessions?

prompts.en: What is something you bought that you still really value?
What experience have you paid for and remembered for a long time?
If someone gave you extra money today, what would you do with it?

reading.title: A New Phone or a Weekend Away?
paragraphs: Imagine you have enough money for one special purchase. You could buy a new phone, a good watch, or a piece of furniture. Or you could spend the same amount on a concert, a short trip, or a meal with people you care about. Which choice gives better value?

A possession is something you can keep. This can be useful because you may use it every day for years. A good bicycle, laptop, or comfortable chair can improve daily life. Some possessions also have emotional value because they were gifts or remind us of important people.

Experiences are different. A holiday or concert ends, but the memory can remain. Psychological research has often found that spending money on experiences can be strongly connected with happiness. One reason may be that experiences are often shared with other people and become part of the stories we tell about our lives.

However, this does not mean buying things is always a bad idea. If you need a reliable laptop for work, spending money on it may reduce stress every day. A trip that causes debt may not feel like money well spent after you return.

There is also another problem: people are different. One person may look back on a weekend in another city for years. Another may receive greater satisfaction from something useful that lasts a long time.
Perhaps the better question is not “things or experiences?” but “What will add the most value to my life after the excitement of paying for it is gone?”

inShort.summary: A **possession** can be useful for years, while an experience may create a lasting **memory**. Research suggests experiences can bring strong **satisfaction**, especially when shared, but the best choice still depends on whether something feels like **money well spent** and what you will **look back on** positively later.

speakingSkill: Comparing lifestyles and making a balanced case

warmup.bigQuestion: Is Working From Home Better Than Working in an Office?

prompts.en: Where do you concentrate best?

What would you miss about an office?

reading.title: Home, Office, or Both?
paragraphs: For many workers, the traditional workday once meant travelling to an office five days a week. Remote work changed that routine. A laptop, internet connection, and online meeting tools now allow many jobs to be done from home.

Working from home can remove the daily commute and give people more flexibility. Someone may have more time for family, exercise, or sleep. Some workers also find it easier to focus at home because there are fewer office interruptions.

But home can create different distractions. Children, housework, noise, or simply the temptation to relax can make concentration difficult. Some remote workers also experience isolation because casual conversations with colleagues disappear. It can become harder to separate work from private life: if your laptop is always nearby, when does the workday really end?

The office offers face-to-face contact and can make teamwork easier. New employees may learn faster when they can ask quick questions in person. However, commuting takes time and money, and open offices can also be noisy and distracting.

OECD survey research with managers and workers across 25 countries found generally positive views of telework and suggested that many respondents saw an arrangement of roughly two or three remote days per week as a useful balance between flexibility and in-person communication.
That does not mean one schedule is best for every worker or every job. A nurse, factory worker, designer, accountant, and software developer face completely different practical realities.
The real question may be less about **where** people work and more about what environment helps them work well without damaging the rest of their lives.

inShort.summary: Remote work can reduce the **commute**, offer more **flexibility**, and improve **work-life balance**, but it may also create **isolation** or new distractions. A **hybrid** arrangement can sometimes help people **get the best of both worlds**.

reading.title: A Useful Tool or Too Much Too Soon?
paragraphs: For many families, giving a child a smartphone feels practical. Parents can call their children, children can contact someone in an emergency, and school information may arrive through apps or messaging groups. A phone can also provide maps, educational videos, cameras, and useful tools.

But owning a smartphone can also mean having almost constant access to social media, games, videos, and strangers online. Parents may worry about screen time, sleep, inappropriate content, privacy, and online pressure.

There is no simple age at which every child suddenly becomes ready. The American Psychological Association notes that adolescents develop at different rates and that age-appropriate social media use should consider maturity, self-control, understanding of risks, and the home environment. This suggests that responsibility may matter as much as a birthday.

Some families set limits. A child may be allowed to use messaging and maps but not social media. Phones may stay outside the bedroom at night, or parents may keep an eye on app use. These rules can reduce some risks, but they also create another question: how much supervision is healthy?
As children get older, they usually expect more privacy and independence. A parent who checks every message may protect a younger child but damage trust with an older teenager.

So the decision is not simply “phone or no phone.” Families also need to decide what kind of access a child should have, which rules are reasonable, and how those rules should change as the child becomes more mature.

inShort.summary: A smartphone can give children useful **access** and help in emergencies, but it also brings online **risks**. Parents may need **supervision**, clear **responsibility**, and rules that **set limits** without **crossing the line** into unnecessary control.

title: Does Social Media Make Friendships Stronger?

warmup.bigQuestion: Does Social Media Make Friendships Stronger?

prompts.en: How often do you communicate with friends online?

reading.title: More Connected, But Are We Closer?
paragraphs: A friend can now be thousands of kilometres away and still feel present in daily life. People share photos, send voice messages, celebrate birthdays online, and reach out when someone needs support. Social media makes it easier to stay in touch even when work, travel, or family life make face-to-face meetings difficult.

Recent Pew Research Center findings show that many U.S. teenagers see friendship as one area where social media can help more than hurt. In its 2025 survey, 30% said social media helped their friendships, while 7% said it hurt them; many others described the effect as neutral.

But frequent contact is not always the same as a meaningful relationship. A person may keep up with hundreds of people online and still have only a few close friends. Social media can also create comparison. Seeing other people’s parties, holidays, or friendships can make someone feel left out.

Communication online also loses some information. A short message can sound angry even when the writer did not mean it that way. Jokes can be misunderstood because we cannot hear tone of voice or see facial expressions.

On the positive side, online communication can help friendships survive distance. People who might slowly drift apart can continue sharing ordinary moments. Someone going through a difficult time can reach out quickly rather than wait for the next meeting.

Social media therefore does not automatically create strong or weak friendships. It is a tool. A friendship may become stronger when people use that tool to communicate honestly and support one another—but weaker when online contact replaces deeper conversation.

inShort.summary: Social media can help people **stay in touch**, **reach out** for **support**, and **keep up with** friends who live far away. But online **comparison** and misunderstanding can damage relationships, and people can still **drift apart** even when they follow each other online.

speakingSkill: Expressing preferences and responding to alternatives

reading.title: A Perfect Plan—or No Plan at All?
paragraphs: Some people feel relaxed when everything is organised. They book restaurants before a trip, make lists before shopping, and know what they will do next weekend by Monday morning. Planning helps them feel prepared and reduces the chance of unpleasant surprises.

Other people dislike detailed schedules. They enjoy making decisions at the last minute, discovering unexpected places, and changing their minds when something more interesting appears. For them, too much planning can make free time feel like another job.

Research on leisure supports this idea in a specific way. In a series of studies, precisely scheduled leisure activities sometimes felt more work-like and less enjoyable, while roughly scheduling an activity—such as choosing an afternoon but not an exact time—helped preserve more of the enjoyment.

Both styles have practical advantages. Planning ahead is useful when tickets sell out, money is limited, or several people need to agree on a time. It can prevent stress because important details are already decided.

Spontaneity can be useful too. Plans sometimes fail because of weather, traffic, illness, or new opportunities. A flexible person may find it easier to adapt instead of feeling that the whole day has been ruined.

The problem appears when one style becomes extreme. Someone who plans every minute may struggle when life changes unexpectedly. Someone who never plans may miss flights, pay higher prices, or create stress for other people.
A balanced approach is to organise what really needs organisation and leave room for surprise. You might book the flight and hotel but decide what to do each afternoon when you arrive.
Perhaps the most useful skill is not planning or spontaneity by itself. It is knowing **when to plan ahead and when to go with the flow**.

inShort.summary: Planning can make people feel **prepared** and reduce **stressful** surprises, while being **flexible** makes it easier to react to the **unexpected**. A balanced person can **plan ahead** but still **go with the flow** when circumstances change.

title: Should People Work Fewer Hours Even If They Earn Less?

warmup.bigQuestion: Should People Work Fewer Hours Even If They Earn Less?

reading.title: More Money or More Time?
paragraphs: Imagine your employer offers you a choice. You can continue working five days a week at your current salary, or work four days and earn 15% less. Which option would you take?

Money clearly matters. People need income for housing, food, transport, healthcare, education, and savings. Someone who is already struggling to make ends meet may not have the freedom to exchange money for time.

However, time also has value. Long working hours can reduce time for sleep, exercise, family, friends, hobbies, and rest. The International Labour Organization has reported that more than one-third of workers globally regularly work more than 48 hours per week, and its research connects unwanted long hours with poorer work-life balance.

Some organisations have experimented with shorter working weeks without cutting salary, often trying to maintain productivity by reducing unnecessary meetings or improving work processes. Results from such trials have attracted attention, but one company’s success does not prove the same model will work in every industry.

There is also an important difference between choosing fewer hours and being unable to find enough paid work. A person working part time by choice may enjoy the extra time. A person who needs more hours to pay rent may experience the same schedule very differently.

The question therefore involves a trade-off. Higher income can create security and opportunity. More free time can improve quality of life. The right answer depends on how much money a person needs, how they value time, and what responsibilities they have.

inShort.summary: Working fewer hours may improve **work-life balance** and **quality of life**, but lower **income** can create financial pressure. Someone who is already trying to **make ends meet** may not be able to **cut down on** work, even if they strongly value more free time.

reading.title: When Easier Is Not Always Better
paragraphs: Modern life is full of services designed to remove effort. Food can arrive at the door, a taxi can appear after two taps, music starts instantly, bills can be paid automatically, and an algorithm can suggest what to watch next.

Convenience saves time and can make important services easier to access. Online markets give people more choice, and digital tools can help people who have limited mobility, live far from shops, or have very busy schedules. OECD work on digital consumer markets highlights both greater convenience and greater choice as major benefits of digitalisation.

But every convenience changes behaviour. If food delivery is always available, a person may cook less. If maps always show the route, people may stop learning their city. If an app remembers every password or decision, we may rely on it without noticing how dependent we have become.

Convenience can also hide costs. A “free” service may use personal data. One-click buying can make spending easier before people have time to think. Recommendation systems can save time but also reduce the chance of discovering something outside our usual interests.
None of this means convenience is bad. Few people want to return to waiting in long lines just because waiting builds patience. The important question is what we gain and what we quietly give up.
Useful convenience removes unnecessary effort. Unhelpful convenience may remove choices, skills, movement, privacy, or moments of reflection that actually matter.
The challenge is noticing the difference before a helpful tool becomes something we cannot imagine living without.

inShort.summary: Convenience can **save time** and put services **at your fingertips**, but it can also increase **dependence** when people **rely on** technology for every small task. We may even **take for granted** tools that quietly change our habits, choices, and privacy.

paragraphs: Generative AI can explain a difficult idea, suggest examples, translate a passage, create practice questions, or give feedback on a first draft. Used carefully, it can act like a tutor that is available at any time. It may also help students who need extra explanations or who are learning in a second language.

The problem is that the same tool can produce an entire assignment in seconds. If a student asks AI to write an essay and then hands it in as personal work, the teacher can no longer see what the student actually knows. This creates an academic-integrity problem and can turn AI from a learning tool into a shortcut.

There is another issue: AI answers are not automatically reliable. A system can produce false information, weak reasoning, or invented sources while sounding confident. Students therefore need to verify important claims rather than take an answer at face value.

UNESCO’s guidance on generative AI in education takes a human-centred approach. It encourages education systems to think about privacy, age, ethics, and the development of human skills rather than treating AI as either completely forbidden or automatically beneficial. UNESCO also stresses the importance of AI literacy for students and teachers.

This suggests that the most useful classroom question may not be “Can students use AI?” but “What kind of use actually supports learning?” Asking AI to explain why an equation is wrong may strengthen understanding. Asking it to complete the whole assignment may remove the learning process itself.

Schools therefore face a difficult policy choice. Rules need to protect genuine student work without pretending that a widely available technology does not exist. The goal is not simply to catch misuse; it is to teach students how to use powerful tools without allowing those tools to do all the thinking for them.

inShort.summary: AI can provide **feedback**, help students produce a **draft**, and support learning, but it can also become a **shortcut** that threatens **academic integrity**. Students need to **verify** information and avoid **taking answers at face value** when AI sounds confident.

reading.title: Can One Birthday Decide When Someone Is Ready?
paragraphs: Many social-media services have minimum-age rules, but the debate is becoming more complicated. Concerns about sleep, harmful content, privacy, bullying, addictive design, and social pressure have led parents and policymakers to ask whether younger users should be kept off some platforms entirely.

Age limits sound simple: choose an age and require platforms to enforce it. Yet enforcement can be difficult. A child can type a false birthday, while stronger age verification may require users to provide identity information or biometric data. A system designed to protect children could therefore create new privacy questions for everyone.

There is also a developmental problem. The American Psychological Association notes that adolescents mature at different rates. It argues that age-appropriate social-media use should consider maturity, self-regulation, understanding of risks, and the home environment. In other words, one age may not perfectly describe every young person’s readiness.

At the same time, leaving the entire decision to individual families may not address platform design. Parents cannot control every recommendation system, notification, or privacy setting. In a 2025 Pew survey, U.S. teens were much more likely to say social media hurt their sleep and productivity than helped them, although views differed across other areas such as friendship.

A strict minimum age could create a clearer safety standard, but it might also give a false sense that everyone above that age is safe. A flexible approach may fit individual maturity better, but it can be harder to enforce consistently.

Age verification creates another practical problem. A platform can ask for a birthday, but that is easy to misreport. Stronger checks may require identity documents, facial estimation, or other personal data. A rule designed to protect privacy and safety can therefore create new privacy questions of its own.

The debate therefore involves more than choosing a number. It requires deciding who should carry responsibility—families, platforms, governments, or young users themselves—and how to protect children without collecting even more personal information about them.

inShort.summary: A minimum **age limit** may reduce some **harmful** exposure, but it can be difficult to **enforce**. Strong **age verification** can create privacy concerns, while differences in **maturity** make a single rule feel **one-size-fits-all**.

reading.title: Degree, Debt, and Opportunity
paragraphs: For generations, university has been presented as a major path to professional opportunity. A degree can provide specialist knowledge, access to careers that require formal qualifications, professional networks, and the chance to study a subject deeply. In many labour markets, graduates also earn more on average than people without a degree.

But “worth it” is not a simple question. Tuition can be expensive, especially where students take out large loans. A degree also has an opportunity cost: years spent studying are years in which a person might otherwise work, build a business, or complete vocational training.

A 2024 Pew Research Center analysis in the United States found mixed public views. Only 22% of adults said a four-year degree was worth the cost even if loans were required, while 47% said it was worth the cost only if a student did not need loans. At the same time, economic data in the report continued to show important differences in outcomes between young adults with and without bachelor’s degrees.

The value also varies by subject, institution, country, and career. Medicine and engineering do not lead to the same opportunities as every other degree, and some high-paying careers can be entered through apprenticeships, technical education, certifications, or experience.
University may also offer benefits that are difficult to measure in salary alone: independence, friendships, exposure to new ideas, research experience, and personal development.

The answer also changes over time. A degree can have value beyond the first salary after graduation, while debt or lost earnings during study can matter immediately. Students therefore need to compare both short-term costs and long-term possibilities rather than treating “university” as one identical product for everyone.

So asking whether university is “worth it” may be too broad. A better question is: **Worth it for whom, for which goal, at what price, and compared with which alternative?** A degree can open doors, but it is no longer sensible to assume that every degree automatically pays off in the same way.

inShort.summary: A university **degree** can **open doors** and improve **career prospects**, but high **tuition** and student **debt** change the calculation. Learners should compare university with alternatives such as **vocational training** and ask whether the investment is likely to **pay off**.

title: Should Edited and AI-Generated Images Be Labelled?

warmup.bigQuestion: Should Edited and AI-Generated Images Be Labelled?

prompts.en: Can you usually tell when an image was generated by AI?
Is normal photo editing different from creating a fake scene?
When does an edited image become misleading?

options.text: Label all meaningful edits and AI-generated images.

options.textAr: Label only content that could mislead people.

reading.title: When Seeing Is No Longer Believing
paragraphs: For much of modern history, photographs have carried a special kind of authority. People know that photos can be staged or edited, but an image still often feels like evidence that something happened. Generative AI is making that assumption harder to maintain.

AI systems can now create realistic people, places, and events that never existed. They can also alter genuine images in ways that are difficult to detect. This can be harmless in art, advertising, or entertainment, but the same technology can be used for impersonation, fraud, or misleading public information.

One response is labelling. From August 2026, European Union AI Act transparency requirements apply to certain AI-generated or manipulated content. Deepfakes must be disclosed, and providers must add machine-readable marks to synthetic content in covered cases. The aim is to reduce deception and help people understand what they are seeing.

But where should the line be drawn? Almost every professional photo may be adjusted for brightness, colour, or framing. Requiring a warning for every small edit could make labels meaningless. On the other hand, only labelling completely invented images may miss important manipulations, such as changing a person’s body, adding someone to a scene, or removing something that changes the meaning.

The form of the label matters as well. A tiny technical marker that ordinary viewers never notice may help automated systems but do little for human understanding. A large warning on harmless creative content may have the opposite problem: it can attract attention without explaining what was actually changed. Useful transparency should communicate the kind and significance of the alteration, not merely announce that “AI was used.”

Labels also do not solve every problem. People may ignore them, they may disappear when content is copied, and bad actors may deliberately remove them. Technical detection and media literacy are still necessary.

The deeper issue is authenticity. Audiences need enough information to judge whether an image represents reality, artistic creation, or deliberate manipulation. The challenge is creating transparency without treating ordinary creative editing as deception.

inShort.summary: AI can create highly realistic but **altered** content, including a **deepfake** that may be **passed off as** real. Clear **disclosure** and **transparency** can protect **authenticity**, but labels need to distinguish meaningful manipulation from ordinary editing.

title: Are Recommendation Algorithms Helping Us or Controlling Us?

warmup.bigQuestion: Are Recommendation Algorithms Helping Us or Controlling Us?

prompts.en: Where do you see recommendations online?

reading.title: Who Chose What You Watched Next?
paragraphs: Open a video app, music service, online shop, or social network and much of what you see has been selected for you. Recommendation algorithms analyse signals such as what you click, watch, buy, skip, like, or search for. They then predict what is most likely to keep your attention or satisfy your preferences.

This can be extremely useful. A person who enjoys a particular kind of music can discover artists from around the world. A shopper can narrow down thousands of products. Someone learning a new skill can quickly find more content at the right level.

However, personalisation changes the environment in which people make choices. The user still clicks, but the platform decides which options appear first. OECD work on digital markets notes that data-driven and algorithmic mechanisms increasingly shape consumer choice, from recommendations to personalised pricing and interface design.

Critics worry that algorithms can filter out unfamiliar perspectives and repeatedly push content similar to what a user already prefers. This may create an echo chamber, although researchers continue to debate how strong such effects are and how much they depend on individual behaviour, platform design, and topic.

This does not mean recommendations are automatically against the user’s interests. The same system can help someone discover a useful book and keep someone scrolling longer than they intended. The result depends partly on what the system is optimising for and whether users can understand or influence that goal.
There is also a commercial incentive. A recommendation does not have to be “best for you” in a broad sense. It may simply be effective at increasing viewing time, purchases, or engagement.

The key issue is control. Personalisation can reduce information overload, but users may not know why they are seeing something or what has been excluded. A useful system should perhaps not only predict preferences but also give people meaningful ways to change those predictions, explore outside them, or turn personalisation down.

inShort.summary: A recommendation **algorithm** can **narrow down** huge amounts of content and create a **personalised** experience. But it can also **filter out** unfamiliar options, **push content** for commercial goals, and potentially create an **echo chamber** if users repeatedly see similar ideas.

reading.title: If You Are Not Paying With Money, What Are You Paying With?
paragraphs: Search engines, social networks, email services, maps, video platforms, and many mobile apps can be used without paying a direct subscription fee. Their business models may instead depend partly on advertising, data analysis, or other commercial uses of user information.

Personal data can make a service more useful. A map remembers favourite places, a music app learns what you enjoy, and advertising may become more relevant. Many users accept some tracking because the service is convenient and free at the point of use.

But meaningful consent is difficult when data collection is complex. People often click “agree” without reading long privacy policies. In a 2023 Pew survey, 56% of U.S. adults said they often or almost always agreed to privacy policies without reading them, and 81% said they were concerned about how companies use collected data.

The issue goes beyond advertising. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission has investigated “surveillance pricing,” where detailed information such as location, browsing behaviour, or shopping history may be used by intermediaries to help tailor prices or promotions. This shows why people may care not only about what information is collected but how it is later used.

Supporters of data-funded services argue that advertising allows useful tools to remain accessible to people who cannot or do not want to pay subscriptions. Critics answer that “free” should not mean unlimited permission to collect, combine, and sell information.

Power matters in this exchange. A user may technically agree to data collection but still have little ability to negotiate the terms. This is especially important when one service dominates a market or when leaving it means losing access to a community, workplace network, or useful digital history.

A fair exchange would therefore require more than a long policy and an “accept” button. Users would need understandable choices, limits on unexpected uses, and a realistic way to opt out without losing every useful feature.

inShort.summary: “Free” digital services often involve **personal data**, **tracking**, and **targeted advertising**. Users may technically give **consent**, but real choice becomes questionable when people cannot easily **opt out** or do not understand what they are **giving away** **in exchange for** access.

title: Could Self-Driving Cars Become Safer Than Human Drivers?

warmup.bigQuestion: Could Self-Driving Cars Become Safer Than Human Drivers?

prompts.en: What causes most driving mistakes?
Would you sleep in a car that was driving itself?

options.text: Perhaps, but only after much more evidence.

reading.title: Removing the Driver From the Crash?
paragraphs: Driving is a complex task. A driver must watch other vehicles, pedestrians, signs, weather, road conditions, and unexpected behaviour while controlling speed and direction. Humans can become tired, distracted, angry, or impaired. Automation offers the possibility of removing some of these weaknesses.

Modern cars already include technologies such as automatic emergency braking, lane warnings, and adaptive cruise control. More advanced systems use cameras, radar, lidar, maps, and software to understand the environment and make driving decisions.

The safety argument is powerful: a mature automated system does not get sleepy, text while driving, or drink alcohol. It may also react faster than a human in some situations. The U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says future higher levels of automation could reduce crashes and human errors.

However, the word “self-driving” can be misleading. NHTSA states that no vehicle currently sold to U.S. consumers is fully self-driving; available systems still require different levels of human attention. A driver who wrongly assumes the system can handle everything may create a new kind of risk.

Automated systems also face difficult edge cases: unusual roadworks, unclear hand signals, extreme weather, or behaviour that was not well represented in training data. A rare software failure could affect many vehicles using the same system.

Responsibility is another problem. If a human driver makes a mistake, responsibility is relatively familiar. If software makes the critical decision, responsibility could involve the passenger, manufacturer, software developer, sensor supplier, or fleet operator.

Trust will also depend on transparency after failure. When a human driver crashes, investigators can examine behaviour and road conditions. Automated systems add software versions, sensors, maps, and decision rules. Clear reporting can help society learn from failures rather than treating every incident as proof that automation is either completely safe or completely unsafe.

The meaningful comparison is therefore not “perfect machine versus imperfect human.” It is whether automated systems, in real conditions and at scale, can achieve a better safety record than human drivers—and whether society knows how to handle the failures that remain.

inShort.summary: An **autonomous** vehicle may reduce some forms of **human error**, but today’s systems still require careful use and possible human **intervention**. Drivers may need to **take over**, systems can **break down**, and unusual **edge cases** make a trustworthy **safety record** essential.

reading.title: Less Meat, Not Necessarily No Meat
paragraphs: Food choices feel personal, but they also have environmental effects. Producing food requires land, water, energy, and transport. Different foods have very different impacts, especially when livestock is involved.

Our World in Data, drawing on major life-cycle research, reports that food systems are responsible for roughly a quarter of global greenhouse-gas emissions. Livestock and fisheries account for a significant share of food emissions, and land used for livestock contributes heavily to food-related land-use emissions. Beef and lamb generally have especially high greenhouse-gas footprints compared with many plant foods.

This has led to calls for people—particularly in high-consuming populations—to cut down on meat. Supporters argue that even partial change can matter. Someone can switch some meals to beans, lentils, vegetables, eggs, or lower-impact animal products without becoming fully vegetarian.

But food is not only an emissions calculation. Diets are connected to culture, tradition, income, health, local agriculture, and access. A policy that feels simple in a wealthy city may look very different in a rural region where livestock is central to livelihoods or nutrition.

Nutrition also matters. Replacing meat with a balanced mixture of other foods is different from simply removing it without considering protein, iron, vitamin B12, or local dietary needs. Environmental arguments are therefore strongest when they avoid pretending that one diet works equally well for every person and place.

There is also an important distinction between meat types and production systems. Saying “meat is bad” hides large differences. Environmental impact can vary significantly by animal, production method, and amount consumed.

The strongest argument for “less meat” is therefore not necessarily that everyone should give it up. It is that people with many food options can consider environmental impact alongside taste, nutrition, price, and culture. The practical question is how much change is realistic—and who should be expected to make it.

But culture, nutrition, income, and individual **carbon footprints** make the issue more complicated than simply **giving up** meat.

reading.title: One Test, Many Meanings
paragraphs: Exams have a powerful advantage: standardisation. If thousands of students answer the same questions under similar conditions, schools and universities can compare results in a way that appears clear and efficient. Standardised tests can also reduce the influence of an individual teacher’s personal opinion.

Yet a test score is not the same thing as ability in general. A student may understand a subject well but perform badly under pressure. Another may be excellent at memorising information but weaker at teamwork, creativity, practical problem solving, or long-term projects.

Fairness is more complicated than giving everyone identical questions. The OECD’s framework for PISA states that fair assessment should not advantage or disadvantage students because of characteristics unrelated to what the test is meant to measure. Test developers therefore examine issues such as cultural bias, language, administration, scoring, and whether questions measure the intended skill.

Socio-economic differences matter too. Students may have different access to tutoring, quiet study spaces, technology, books, or schools with experienced teachers. A perfectly standardised exam cannot automatically create a level playing field outside the examination room.

The purpose of the assessment should also shape the method. A short exam may be useful for checking knowledge under the same conditions, while a practical task may reveal how well someone can apply that knowledge. Fairness may therefore require matching the assessment to the skill being measured rather than searching for one perfect format.

However, alternatives are not automatically fairer. Teacher assessment can be influenced by unconscious bias. Portfolios require time to evaluate. Interviews may reward confident speakers. Group projects make it difficult to separate individual contributions.

The strongest case may therefore be for using several forms of assessment rather than expecting one test to answer every question. An exam can provide useful evidence, especially when designed carefully, but it should be interpreted as one measure of performance—not a complete description of a person’s intelligence, potential, or worth.

inShort.summary: A **standardised** exam can measure some forms of **ability** consistently, but fairness also requires attention to **bias** and whether students **perform under pressure**. Identical testing conditions do not automatically create a **level playing field**, so multiple forms of **assessment** may provide a fuller picture.

reading.title: Where Did All the Saved Time Go?
paragraphs: A message that once took days to arrive can now be delivered in seconds. Banking can be completed from a phone, documents can be searched instantly, meetings can happen across continents, and software can automate repetitive tasks. By almost any technical measure, many activities are faster than they used to be.

Yet many people do not feel surrounded by spare time. Faster communication can create faster expectations. If a message arrives instantly, people may expect an instant reply. If a worker can log in from anywhere, work can follow them home. Technology can free up ten minutes and then fill those ten minutes with notifications, updates, and new tasks.

This is sometimes called a rebound effect: efficiency reduces the time or cost of an activity, but people respond by doing more of it. Faster email did not necessarily create less communication; it made sending far more messages practical.

Digital tools also make multitasking tempting. Someone can answer a work message while watching television and checking a delivery app. This can feel efficient, but switching attention repeatedly may also make the day feel fragmented.

On the other hand, it would be strange to deny the real benefits. Navigation, online payments, washing machines, search engines, and automated systems genuinely remove effort and save time. The issue may be what society does with the time that is saved.

Workplace expectations are especially important. The International Labour Organization has argued for clearer boundaries in telework and the ability to disconnect during rest periods. A time-saving technology does not guarantee more free time if organisations simply increase the amount of work expected.

This is why the same tool can feel liberating to one person and exhausting to another. A messaging app may remove a commute to a meeting, yet also make colleagues expect instant replies. The effect depends partly on social rules around the technology, not only on the device itself.
Technology therefore changes both capability and expectation. It can make each task faster while allowing more tasks to enter the same day.

inShort.summary: Technology can improve **efficiency**, **speed up** routine tasks, and **free up** time. But faster communication can also raise **expectations**, make work feel **always-on**, and allow tasks to **pile up** until the saved time disappears.
